title: Cell Cycle and Cell Division
tagline: Interphase, mitosis and meiosis: how cells copy and halve their chromosomes.

overview.intro: This chapter explains how a cell duplicates its contents and then divides, first by mitosis to give two identical daughter cells, then by meiosis to halve the chromosome number for sexual reproduction. The cell cycle and its phases come first, then the stages of mitosis with what happens to the chromosomes in each, then meiosis as two successive divisions, and finally the comparison between the two that every examination paper asks for. The examiners’ three standing demands are to name the phase in which a given event occurs, to draw and label the stages, and to explain why meiosis is necessary for sexual reproduction.

facts.label: Interphase
facts.value: G1 for growth and protein synthesis, S for DNA replication, G2 for preparation — the cell spends about 90 per cent of its time here.

facts.label: Mitosis
facts.value: Prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase followed by cytokinesis, giving two genetically identical diploid cells.

facts.label: Meiosis
facts.value: Two divisions with a single replication, giving four haploid cells with crossing over and independent assortment.

facts.label: Significance of meiosis
facts.value: Halves the chromosome number so fertilisation restores it, and creates new combinations by crossing over and independent assortment.

learningOutcomes: Describe the phases of the cell cycle and state what occurs in each.
Trace the behaviour of chromosomes through mitosis and cytokinesis.
Explain meiosis I and meiosis II, including crossing over and independent assortment.
Compare mitosis and meiosis under standard headings.
State the significance of each type of division with examples.

blocks.text: The cell cycle is the ordered sequence of events a cell passes through between one division and the next, and it is divided into interphase, the period of growth and preparation, and the mitotic phase, division itself. Interphase occupies about ninety per cent of the cycle and is split into three stages. In G1, the first gap, the cell grows, synthesises proteins and increases its organelles, and it is here that a cell not destined to divide leaves the cycle and enters G0, a resting state in which it carries out its function without dividing — nerve and muscle cells remain in G0, which is why adult nerve tissue does not regenerate. In S phase, synthesis, each chromosome is replicated so that the two identical copies, called sister chromatids, are joined at the centromere; the amount of DNA in the nucleus therefore doubles while the chromosome number stays the same, so a cell that begins with 46 chromosomes still has 46, each now consisting of two chromatids. In G2, the second gap, the cell grows further and synthesises the proteins needed for division, particularly the tubulin of which spindle fibres are made, and it checks that replication was complete. The mitotic phase follows: the nucleus divides by mitosis and the cytoplasm by cytokinesis, giving two daughter cells that each re-enter G1. Two checkpoints govern the cycle: the G1 checkpoint commits the cell to division only if its DNA is undamaged and conditions suit, and the G2 checkpoint confirms that replication is complete before mitosis begins, while a spindle checkpoint during mitosis waits until every chromosome is properly attached to the spindle. If damage cannot be repaired the cell leaves the cycle and undergoes apoptosis, programmed cell death, which protects the organism from a cell with faulty instructions — the failure of these checkpoints is a step towards cancer, in which cells divide without observing the normal controls.

items: Interphase consists of G1 growth, S replication and G2 preparation, and occupies about ninety per cent of the cycle.
In S phase the DNA replicates, so each chromosome has two sister chromatids joined at the centromere.
The chromosome number does not double in S phase; the DNA content does.
Cells that leave the cycle enter G0, as nerve and muscle cells do, and may never divide again.
Checkpoints at G1, G2 and the spindle monitor DNA damage and replication before allowing division.
Failure of checkpoints lets a cell divide with damaged DNA, a step on the road to cancer.
Apoptosis removes cells whose instructions are faulty rather than letting them persist.

items.text: Why the nucleus looks the same in S phase
items.note: Chromosomes duplicate without becoming twice as numerous, so a stained nucleus shows the same count before and after replication.
Most nerve cells sit permanently in G0, so the tissue has no dividing cells with which to repair a cut.

blocks.text: Mitosis is the division of the nucleus that produces two nuclei genetically identical to the parent, and it proceeds through four named stages followed by the division of the cytoplasm. In prophase the chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes, each already replicated as two chromatids held at the centromere; the nucleolus disappears; the nuclear envelope breaks down; and the centrosomes, which duplicated during interphase, move to opposite poles and send out microtubules that form the spindle, with kinetochores developing at the centromeres ready to attach. In metaphase the chromosomes are drawn to the centre of the cell and align along the equatorial plate, an imaginary plane equidistant from the poles, with spindle fibres from each pole attached to the kinetochores of each chromosome; this is the stage at which chromosomes are counted and photographed, because they are at their most condensed, and the alignment ensures that each daughter cell will receive one chromatid of every pair. In anaphase the centromeres divide and the sister chromatids are pulled apart by the shortening of the spindle fibres, each chromatid now counted as a full chromosome, and they travel to opposite poles; the cell elongates as the polar microtubules slide past one another. In telophase the chromosomes arrive at the poles and begin to decondense back into chromatin, a nuclear envelope re-forms around each group, and the nucleolus reappears. Cytokinesis then divides the cytoplasm: in animal cells a cleavage furrow forms as a contractile ring of actin pinches the cell in two, while in plant cells vesicles from the Golgi collect at the centre and fuse to form a cell plate that grows outwards into a new cell wall. Mitosis is universal in growth, in the replacement of worn tissue such as the lining of the gut and the skin, and in asexual reproduction, and its significance lies in exactness: the daughter cells receive an identical set of chromosomes, so the genetic constitution of the organism is preserved in every cell that divides this way.

items: Prophase: chromatin condenses, nucleolus disappears, envelope breaks down and the spindle forms.
Metaphase: chromosomes align on the equatorial plate with spindle fibres attached to kinetochores.
Anaphase: centromeres divide and sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles, becoming separate chromosomes.
Telophase: chromosomes decondense, nuclear envelopes re-form and nucleoli reappear.
Cytokinesis: a cleavage furrow pinches animal cells; a cell plate builds a wall in plant cells.
Mitosis gives two daughter cells genetically identical to the parent and to each other.
It underlies growth, tissue repair and asexual reproduction.
Metaphase is the stage for counting chromosomes, since they are maximally condensed and aligned.

blocks.caption: Stages of mitosis
rows: furrow in animals, cell plate in plants

items.note: Bone marrow cells divide continuously by mitosis to replace the blood cells that wear out after a few months of circulation.
Cells at the edge leave G0, pass through the cycle and divide by mitosis, so the new tissue carries the same DNA as the old.

blocks.text: Meiosis is the division that halves the chromosome number, producing four haploid cells from one diploid cell, and it does so with only one replication of DNA and two successive divisions. Meiosis I, the reduction division, begins with prophase I, the longest and most important stage: the homologous chromosomes pair up by a process called synapsis to form bivalents, and while paired they exchange segments in crossing over, in which non-sister chromatids break and rejoin, so that each chromatid carries a mixture of maternal and paternal material; the nuclear envelope then breaks down and the spindle forms. In metaphase I the bivalents align at the equator with each pair oriented at random, so maternal and paternal chromosomes of each pair are distributed independently — this independent assortment, together with crossing over, is the source of genetic variation. In anaphase I homologous chromosomes separate, whole chromosomes moving to opposite poles while the sister chromatids remain joined at their centromeres, which is the step that halves the chromosome number. Telophase I and cytokinesis then give two cells, each with half the chromosomes but each chromosome still doubled. Meiosis II resembles mitosis: in prophase II the spindle re-forms, in metaphase II the chromosomes align individually at the equator, in anaphase II the centromeres divide and the chromatids separate, and telophase II with cytokinesis yields four haploid daughter cells, each with a single chromatid per chromosome. The significance of meiosis is threefold. It halves the chromosome number so that fertilisation, the fusion of two gametes, restores the diploid number instead of doubling it each generation. It generates new combinations of genes through crossing over in prophase I and independent assortment in metaphase I, which is why offspring of sexual reproduction differ from their parents and from one another. And it provides the haploid gametes that sexual reproduction requires, with the variation it introduces giving natural selection something to act upon.

items: One replication is followed by two divisions, giving four haploid cells from one diploid cell.
Prophase I: homologous chromosomes pair as bivalents and undergo crossing over.
Metaphase I: bivalents align at random, giving independent assortment of maternal and paternal chromosomes.
Anaphase I: homologues separate while sister chromatids stay joined — this halves the chromosome number.
Meiosis II separates the chromatids, as mitosis does, giving four haploid cells.
Meiosis halves the number so fertilisation can restore it rather than doubling it each generation.
Crossing over and independent assortment together create genetic variation.
The four cells are not identical, unlike the two cells produced by mitosis.

four haploid cells with single chromatids

items.note: Crossing over in prophase I and the random orientation of bivalents in metaphase I mean each gamete carries a different mixture of the parents’ chromosomes.
A human egg or sperm carries 23 chromosomes, so fertilisation restores 46 rather than raising the number to 92.

items.meaning: The growth and replication period of G1, S and G2 before division.
Identical copies of a replicated chromosome joined at the centromere.
Exchange of segments between homologous chromatids in prophase I.
The random orientation of homologous pairs at metaphase I.

learn.title: Comparing mitosis and meiosis, and why each matters

blocks.text: Mitosis and meiosis are best compared by asking four questions of each: how many divisions take place, what separates, how many cells result, and are the cells alike. Mitosis consists of one division and separates sister chromatids, giving two cells that are diploid and genetically identical to the parent; meiosis consists of two divisions, separating homologues first and chromatids second, giving four cells that are haploid and genetically distinct from one another and from the parent. The pairing and crossing over that occur in meiosis have no counterpart in mitosis, and the random orientation of bivalents in metaphase I likewise has none. Functionally the two answer different needs: mitosis builds and maintains the body, replacing worn cells and growing tissue while preserving the exact chromosome constitution, whereas meiosis produces the gametes and spores of sexual reproduction and reduces the chromosome number so that fertilisation can restore it. A useful way to hold the distinction is that mitosis preserves, while meiosis diversifies. Two practical points round off the topic. Errors matter: if a pair of homologues fails to separate in anaphase I, a gamete carries an extra or missing chromosome, and the resulting condition — trisomy 21 in Down syndrome being the standard example — shows how precisely meiosis must run. And the two divisions must be distinguished by what separates at each: whole chromosomes in anaphase I and individual chromatids in anaphase II, which is the point on which most comparison questions turn.

items: Mitosis: one division, chromatids separate, two diploid identical cells.
Meiosis: two divisions, homologues then chromatids separate, four haploid distinct cells.
Pairing, crossing over and independent assortment occur only in meiosis.
Mitosis preserves the chromosome constitution; meiosis halves it and creates variation.
Failure of chromosomes to separate, called nondisjunction, gives gametes with an extra or missing chromosome.
Trisomy 21, Down syndrome, results from an extra chromosome 21 at fertilisation.
Anaphase I separates whole chromosomes; anaphase II separates chromatids.

items.note: A skin cell divides by mitosis so every cell carries the same instructions; a sperm cell comes from meiosis so each carries half the chromosomes and a new combination of genes.
One chromosome too many in a gamete produces a viable but affected child, which is why the checkpoints of meiosis matter so much.

keyPoints: The cell cycle is interphase followed by the mitotic phase of mitosis and cytokinesis.
Interphase consists of G1 growth, S replication and G2 preparation and occupies about ninety per cent of the cycle.
DNA replicates in S phase but the chromosome number does not change.
Checkpoints at G1, G2 and the spindle prevent a damaged cell from dividing.
Prophase condenses chromosomes and forms the spindle; metaphase aligns them at the equator.
Anaphase separates sister chromatids; telophase re-forms the nuclei; cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm.
Animal cells divide by a cleavage furrow and plant cells by a cell plate.
Meiosis has two divisions after a single replication, giving four haploid cells.
Crossing over in prophase I and independent assortment in metaphase I generate genetic variation.
Meiosis halves the chromosome number so that fertilisation restores it.
Mitosis produces identical cells for growth and repair; meiosis produces gametes.
Nondisjunction in meiosis produces gametes with an extra or missing chromosome.
examFocus: Stage questions must state what the chromosomes do, not only what the cell does.
The comparison table expects divisions, cells produced, chromosome number, what separates and purpose.
Significance of meiosis wants three points: restoration at fertilisation, variation, and gamete production.
Labelled diagrams of mitosis and of meiosis I are frequently drawn from memory.

Identical halves of a replicated chromosome joined at the centromere.
The protein structure at a centromere to which spindle fibres attach.
The pairing of homologous chromosomes during prophase I.
Exchange of segments between homologous chromatids producing new combinations.
Random orientation of homologous pairs giving new combinations in gametes.

Programmed cell death that removes damaged cells safely.

questions.prompt: DNA replication occurs during which phase of the cell cycle?
questions.explanation: S phase is synthesis, when each chromosome is copied into two sister chromatids.

questions.prompt: During which stage of mitosis do chromosomes align at the equatorial plate?
questions.explanation: Metaphase alignment lets spindle fibres from both poles attach before separation.
Homologous chromatids exchange segments while paired as bivalents in prophase I.

questions.prompt: How many cells are produced at the end of meiosis and what is their chromosome number?
questions.explanation: Meiosis gives four haploid cells, each with one chromosome of each pair.

questions.prompt: The contractile ring that pinches an animal cell in two during cytokinesis is made of the protein __________.
questions.explanation: Plant cells cannot form a furrow, so they build a cell plate instead.

questions.prompt: The pairing of homologous chromosomes during prophase I is called __________.
questions.explanation: Synapsis forms bivalents and permits crossing over between non-sister chromatids.

questions.prompt: What is meant by the G0 phase and give an example of a cell in it.
questions.answer: The G0 phase is a resting state in which a cell has left the active cell cycle and no longer prepares to divide, but remains metabolically active and carries out its specialised function. Cells enter G0 either temporarily, when a quiescent cell such as a liver cell may re-enter the cycle after injury, or permanently, as neurons and mature muscle cells do. Because such cells do not divide, tissue composed of them cannot be replaced by mitosis after damage, which is why an injury to the spinal cord produces permanent loss of function.
questions.explanation: Definition of G0 as left the cycle but metabolically active, with a temporary and a permanent example and the consequence.

questions.prompt: Describe what happens during anaphase of mitosis.
questions.answer: At the start of anaphase the centromeres that hold the sister chromatids together divide, and the kinetochores of each chromatid are gripped by spindle fibres from the opposite pole. The shortening of the kinetochore fibres draws the chromatids apart, each moving towards the pole to which its fibre is attached, so that identical sets of chromosomes travel to the two ends of the cell. At this moment each separated chromatid is counted as an individual chromosome. Meanwhile the polar microtubules lengthen and slide past one another, elongating the cell and drawing the poles further apart, so that the two future daughter cells are physically separated before telophase begins.
questions.explanation: Centromere division, chromatids drawn to opposite poles by shortening fibres, the change of status to chromosomes, and cell elongation.

questions.prompt: State two differences between mitosis and meiosis.
questions.answer: Mitosis consists of a single division and separates sister chromatids to produce two diploid cells that are genetically identical to the parent, whereas meiosis consists of two successive divisions and separates homologous chromosomes first and chromatids second, producing four haploid cells. Secondly, pairing of homologous chromosomes, crossing over and independent assortment occur only in meiosis, so the four cells produced are all genetically different, while the two cells produced by mitosis are alike.
questions.explanation: Any two of: number of divisions, number and ploidy of products, what separates, genetic identity, or presence of pairing and crossing over.

questions.prompt: Explain the significance of meiosis in sexual reproduction.
questions.answer: Meiosis matters first because it halves the chromosome number. A diploid organism has two of every chromosome, and if gametes were also diploid, the fusion of two at fertilisation would double the number in every generation, so the species would grow more chromosomally unstable with each generation. Meiosis produces gametes with one chromosome from each pair, so fertilisation restores exactly the diploid number of the parents and the chromosome count stays constant across generations. Second, meiosis generates genetic variation, and it does so by two mechanisms. In prophase I homologous chromosomes pair and exchange segments in crossing over, so each chromatid carries a mixture of maternal and paternal material that did not exist in either parent. In metaphase I the bivalents align at random, so the maternal chromosome of one pair and the paternal chromosome of another may go to the same pole in any combination; with 23 pairs in humans this independent assortment alone allows more than eight million possible combinations in a single gamete. Third, meiosis produces the haploid cells that sexual reproduction requires, and the variation they carry gives natural selection the differences on which it acts. The result is that offspring differ from their parents and from one another, which is the raw material of evolution.
questions.explanation: Halving so fertilisation restores it, variation by crossing over and independent assortment, and the production of gametes with evolutionary consequence.

questions.prompt: A cell is observed with its chromosomes aligned at the equator, each chromosome consisting of two chromatids joined at the centromere, with spindle fibres attached. Identify the division taking place and stage, and explain how the outcome would differ if this were meiosis instead of mitosis.
questions.answer: Chromosomes aligned at the equator with spindle fibres attached to their centromeres and each still composed of two chromatids identifies metaphase, and because each chromosome is aligned individually rather than as a paired bivalent, the division is mitosis. In mitotic metaphase the purpose of the alignment is that the kinetochores of both sister chromatids face opposite poles, so when the centromeres divide in anaphase each chromatid is drawn to a different pole and the two daughter cells receive exactly the same set of chromosomes as the parent. If this were meiosis instead, the stage would differ according to which division was meant. In metaphase I of meiosis the chromosomes would be aligned as homologous pairs, with each bivalent attached so that whole chromosomes face opposite poles, and the separation in anaphase I would send one entire chromosome of each pair to each pole while the chromatids stayed joined — halving the number. In metaphase II the alignment would look much like mitotic metaphase, but the cells would already be haploid, so the separation in anaphase II would give four haploid cells rather than two diploid ones. The distinction therefore rests on whether homologues are paired and on how many divisions follow.
questions.explanation: Mitotic metaphase identified with the reasoning, then the meiotic contrast for metaphase I and metaphase II, with the chromosome numbers in each outcome.

questions.prompt: Explain why cancer is described as a disease of the cell cycle, and describe how the normal controls prevent it.
questions.answer: Cancer cells divide without observing the controls that normally govern the cell cycle, so the disease can be understood directly as a failure of those controls. Normally a cell proceeds through G1 only if conditions are suitable and its DNA is undamaged: a checkpoint at the end of G1 inspects the DNA and, if damage is found, halts the cycle so repair enzymes can act, and if the damage cannot be repaired the cell is triggered into apoptosis, destroying itself rather than passing faulty instructions on. A second checkpoint before mitosis confirms that replication in S phase was complete and that no DNA remains damaged, and a spindle checkpoint waits until every chromosome is properly attached to spindle fibres before anaphase begins, preventing chromosomes from being lost. Cancer arises when mutations disable these checkpoints or the genes that enforce them — the proto-oncogenes that normally signal division become oncogenes that signal it constantly, while the tumour suppressor genes that halt the cycle cease to function. The cell then divides autonomously, ignores signals to stop, evades apoptosis and may recruit new blood supply, producing a tumour. Understanding cancer as a cell cycle problem explains both why it becomes more common with age, as mutations accumulate through repeated divisions, and why many treatments work by interrupting the cycle at a particular phase.
questions.explanation: Normal checkpoints described with what each detects, then the failure of proto-oncogenes and tumour suppressors, and the consequences.
